items.headline: Disney beats with $25.9B in sales and raises its dividend 33% to $2 a year
items.caption: Disney's revenue rose 16% and adjusted profit of $1.77 a share topped the $1.67 forecast. The stock rose about 2% before the open.

visual.foot: Dividend paid in January and July

detail: Disney reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $25.9 billion, up 16%. Adjusted earnings were $1.77 a share, ahead of the $1.67 analysts expected.
The company raised its annual dividend by a third, to $2 a share, paid as two $1 checks in January and July. Shares rose about 2.15% to $121.25 in early trading.
Streaming did well. Disney+ and Hulu earned $824 million, more than double a year ago, on revenue up 19% to $6.05 billion.
money: A bigger dividend means more cash for shareholders, but check the yield before buying just for income.
If you own Disney through an index fund, a beat like this helps your fund a little, not a lot.
Streaming profits rising can mean fewer price cuts on Disney+ plans; compare bundles before renewing.

For fiscal 2027, Disney guided to about 8% operating income growth, double-digit adjusted EPS growth and about $11 billion in free cash flow. It expects roughly $9 billion of buybacks in the first quarter.

Big buybacks reduce share count, which can lift earnings per share for long-term holders.

items.headline: US requires licenses for top AI chips in 5 countries, from Malaysia to Brazil
items.caption: A new rule bans remote access to certain AI chips in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil. The goal is to stop Chinese firms renting that power.

visual.title: The new chip rule
items: Covers Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Brazil
License needed to sell top AI chips and servers there
Bans remote access to certain GPUs in those data centers
Exempts shopping and social media recommender systems
Issued as an interim final rule by Commerce

detail: The Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security now requires a license to sell the most advanced AI chips and servers into five countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil.

The rule also bans remote access to certain GPUs and servers in data centers there. US officials say Chinese tech firms had been renting computing power in these hubs to train AI models. Systems used for retail and social media recommendations are exempt.
An analyst told The Register the rule may shift the compliance burden onto data center and cloud operators. Separately, the US confirmed a criminal probe into Singapore's Megaspeed.
money: Chip stocks can swing on export news; avoid piling into one chipmaker before Nvidia's results.
Broad index funds spread export-rule risk across many companies.
Cloud firms with US-only data centers may gain if rentals shift away from these hubs.
risk: More rules could follow, and markets in Asia and Europe already fell on the news.

Small businesses can use voice AI tools to cut call center and translation costs.

The work rules for HUSKY D, the state's adult Medicaid group, still begin Jan. 1. Enrollees need 80 hours a month of work, school, service or training, or must earn at least $580 a month. Some people are exempt.
The rules came from the 2025 federal tax and spending law. State leaders hope the new Congress repeals them, but that would need Trump's support.

Check if you qualify for an exemption. It can save you from paperwork later.

detail: More states are 'decoupling' from parts of the 2025 federal tax law rather than raising income tax rates, according to Thomson Reuters' Checkpoint. That means they don't follow certain federal deductions when figuring state tax.

The most common change: spreading out write-offs for 100% bonus depreciation and domestic research costs over more years. Democratic-leaning states appear more likely to do this. Some states also tax a type of foreign profit, called NCTI, often without a foreign tax credit.
Budget pressure is part of the story. Starting in fiscal 2027, the federal share of SNAP administrative costs drops from 50% to 25%, shifting costs to states.
money: Small business owners: your state write-off may differ from your federal one; ask your preparer.

detail: Aon said Monday it completed its $17 billion deal for USI, announced in August. USI is based in Valhalla, New York, with about $3 billion in yearly revenue, more than 10,500 employees and nearly 200 offices.
Together, Aon, NFP and USI's middle-market units bring in about $6.5 billion a year. Aon expects $395 million in net cost and revenue gains, and it gets wider access to specialty insurance markets.
KKR, which bought USI with CPPIB in 2017 for $4.3 billion, says it netted about $3.3 billion after tax. Aon will update its 2027 outlook with fourth-quarter results.
money: If your business buys insurance through USI, ask whether your broker, service team or carriers will change.
Broker consolidation can reduce choice; get a competing quote at your next renewal.
Insurance brokers earn steady fees, which is why private equity and big firms keep buying them.
risk: Integration problems could disrupt service for clients.
The article does not detail any job changes.

items.headline: Justice Dept. will review DoorDash's $17 billion Instacart deal, sources say
items.caption: Antitrust officials will study the grocery delivery merger. DoorDash owes Instacart $1.25 billion if regulators block it.

items.t: Groups urge FTC to block it

detail: The Justice Department will handle the antitrust review of DoorDash's planned purchase of Instacart, two people familiar with the matter said Monday. A DOJ spokesperson declined to comment on the deal.
DoorDash agreed in October to buy Instacart for about $17 billion to grow in US grocery delivery. It agreed to pay Instacart $1.25 billion if the deal fails antitrust review.
Regulators can approve a deal, negotiate conditions, or sue to block it. The department says it will keep focusing on affordability and competition. No review timeline was given.
money: If you order groceries through either app, compare fees and memberships now; a merger could change pricing.
Delivery drivers who work both apps may see changes in pay or availability if the deal closes.
Merger arbitrage bets carry real risk when regulators step in.
risk: A long review could delay or kill the deal.
Conditions might force sales of some business lines.

items.headline: Mercedes freezes new investment at German plants and warns some could close
items.caption: The carmaker wants to save about EUR 800 million and is shifting more work abroad, including the GLC SUV to Alabama in late 2027.

visual.title: Mercedes' German squeeze
items: Board halts future investment at German sites
Seeks ~EUR 800M savings; may lift work week from 35 to 38 hours
About 108,000 German workers, two-thirds of its staff
GLC SUV assembly moving to the US in late 2027

detail: Mercedes-Benz's board has stopped all future investment at its German sites, production chief Michael Schiebe said, according to the Telegraph. The company is weighing which German plants it can still afford.

It wants to save about EUR 800 million, partly by raising the work week from 35 to at least 38 hours and possibly trimming holiday bonuses. The IG Metall union opposes the plan. About 108,000 people, two-thirds of its staff, work in Germany.

Mercedes cut its 2026 profit margin forecast to 2% to 3%, and China sales fell 8% last quarter. To avoid US tariffs it is moving GLC assembly to the US in late 2027 and spending $4 billion on its Tuscaloosa, Alabama plant.
money: More US assembly could add jobs at Alabama suppliers and steady US prices for some models.
European automakers face weak margins; if you own them, weigh that against dividend yields.
Car shoppers may find deals on imported models as makers fight for sales.
risk: A long union fight could disrupt production.
Plant closures would hit German suppliers and towns.

items.headline: 13F filings show 7 big banks held about $29M in XRP funds; Intesa leads with $27M
items.caption: JPMorgan, Bank of America and Morgan Stanley held tiny stakes. Spot XRP ETFs lost $19M in outflows last week.

visual.title: Bank XRP ETF stakes (Sept. 30)
visual.foot: Jane Street held $23.5M in XRP-linked funds.

detail: Quarterly 13F holdings reports, due Monday, show seven banks together held about $29.4 million in XRP exchange-traded funds as of Sept. 30.

Italy's Intesa Sanpaolo was by far the largest, with about $27.2 million across Grayscale and Bitwise XRP funds. UBS held $1.91 million. Morgan Stanley, Bank of America and JPMorgan held stakes between about $9,000 and $116,000.
Trading firm Jane Street reported $23.5 million in XRP-linked funds. Separately, US spot XRP ETFs had $19.13 million in net withdrawals from Nov. 9 to 13.
money: Tiny bank stakes often come from client trades or market making, not big bets; don't read them as endorsements.
If you want crypto exposure, check an ETF's fees and whether it holds spot coins or futures.
Keep any crypto slice small enough that a 40% drop would not derail your plans.
risk: XRP is already about 40% below its October highs.
13F data is weeks old and misses later trades.

items.headline: Stablecoin supply shrinks $4.15B in a week as traders pull cash from crypto
items.caption: Total stablecoins fell to about $285B, down 5% in a month. Leveraged DEX trading jumped 15% during the selloff.
detail: Total stablecoin market value dropped by $4.15 billion over the week of Nov. 9 to 15, according to Lookonchain. DeFiLlama puts the total at $284.91 billion, down 1.43% in a week and 5.17% in a month.
Tether fell 0.83% to about $175 billion and USDC fell 1.73% to about $69 billion. Shrinking stablecoin supply often means money leaving crypto rather than waiting to buy.
Trading still picked up. Weekly perpetual futures volume on decentralized exchanges rose 14.67% to $188 billion, led by Hyperliquid. Publicly traded companies were net sellers of 11,182 bitcoin.
money: Falling stablecoin supply is a sign of weaker buying power; be cautious about calling a bottom.
If you hold stablecoins for yield, know who backs them and how quickly you can cash out.
Avoid leverage in volatile weeks; liquidations can wipe out positions fast.
risk: Outflows can continue if prices keep falling.
Data providers measure supply differently.

items.headline: Social Security letters warn some Medicare enrollees coverage may end Feb. 1
items.caption: People whose eligibility under a 2025 law can't be confirmed must send proof by the date in their letter. Social Security checks are not affected.

items.t: New law limits Medicare by status

detail: Social Security began writing on Nov. 10 to people on Medicare whose eligibility it cannot confirm under a law passed in July 2025. The letters say Medicare may end Feb. 1, 2027, unless they prove they still qualify by the date given.

Eligible groups include US citizens and nationals, green card holders, Cuban-Haitian entrants and certain Pacific island compact citizens. Refugees, asylees, TPS holders and humanitarian parolees lose Medicare unless they also fit one of those groups.
Documents can be uploaded through my Social Security or brought to an office. The help line is 1-844-507-7131. Social Security says its cash benefits do not change.
money: If you or a relative gets a letter, respond before the deadline to avoid a gap in coverage.
Use my Social Security to upload papers and keep a copy of what you send.
People who lose Medicare this way can't get Marketplace subsidies, so plan for full-price costs.
risk: Missing the letter's deadline could mean losing coverage Feb. 1.
Some online write-ups cite a wrong Jan. 4 date.

items.headline: Senators file a Medicare-at-50 buy-in bill; the deadline that counts now is Dec. 15
items.caption: The bill would let people 50 to 64 buy Medicare with subsidies, but it isn't law. For Jan. 1 coverage, pick a HealthCare.gov plan by Dec. 15.
detail: Sen. Tammy Baldwin and nine colleagues introduced the Medicare at 50 Act on Nov. 10. It would let people ages 50 to 64 buy into Medicare Parts A, B and D, with Marketplace-style tax credits to help with costs.
The plan is optional and has not passed Congress, so there is no start date. A separate idea to lower the age to 55 comes from Sen. Bernie Sanders.
For now, HealthCare.gov shoppers must choose a plan by Dec. 15 for coverage starting Jan. 1, or by Jan. 15 for Feb. 1. Medicare open enrollment ends Dec. 7. Some state marketplaces run longer.
money: Don't wait on this bill; pick 2027 coverage by the Dec. 15 deadline.
If a spouse under 65 is on your work plan, confirm what happens to their coverage when you retire.
Compare Marketplace plans every year; subsidy amounts and networks change.
risk: The bill may never pass.
Missing Dec. 15 can mean a gap in January coverage.

items.headline: New Mexico plan: one 4.7% income tax rate, and about 266,000 filers would owe nothing
items.caption: A key House chair wants to replace six brackets with a flat rate plus a shrinking credit. It would cost about $729M a year.

visual.title: New Mexico income tax
visual.foot: Credit phases out at $175K single / $350K married. Session starts Jan. 19.

detail: Rep. Derrick Lente, who chairs New Mexico's House tax committee, proposed a single 4.7% personal income tax rate. A credit that shrinks as income rises would cover singles earning up to $175,000 and couples up to $350,000.
Today the state has six brackets from 1.5% to 5.9%. Lente says about 266,000 filers, nearly a quarter of returns, would effectively owe no state income tax, and nearly everyone would pay less.

An analysis puts the cost at $729 million in the 2029 budget year. Other ideas include a one-time $250 rebate from the governor and plans from Governor-elect Deb Haaland. The 60-day session starts Jan. 19.
money: New Mexico residents: no change yet, so file 2026 taxes under current brackets.
Lower-income filers stand to gain most if the credit passes; watch the January session.
If you're weighing a move, state income tax is only one part; check property and sales taxes too.
risk: The plan could change or fail in the Legislature.
Lost revenue could squeeze state programs.

sources.t: New Mexico income tax overhaul proposal would cut taxes for most residents

items.headline: New: California's next insurance chief will review the rules that let insurers raise rates
items.caption: Jane Kim says Lara's Sustainable Insurance Strategy favors insurers and wants clearer rate filings. Insurers warn against undoing progress.

visual.title: What Kim plans
items: Review Lara's faster rate reviews and catastrophe-model pricing
More transparent rate filings and quicker claims payment
Home and auto insurance as early priorities
Transition team for her first 100 days
Mercury pledged 38,000 new policies under the current rules

detail: What's new: Commissioner-elect Jane Kim says she will examine Ricardo Lara's Sustainable Insurance Strategy, which speeds rate reviews and lets insurers price in catastrophe models and reinsurance costs in return for writing more policies in fire areas.
Kim says the approach tilts toward insurers. She wants more open rate filings and faster claims payment, and is forming a transition team of insurance, climate and tech experts.

Under the current rules, Farmers lifted its policy cap and Mercury pledged 38,000 new policies, while CSAA and Mercury got 6.9% rate hikes. Industry groups urged her not to reverse recent gains or prejudge filings.
money: California homeowners: shop your policy at renewal, since more insurers are writing again.
Ask your insurer about discounts for wildfire mitigation work on your home.
Watch for rate filing changes in 2027; they could affect how fast premiums rise.
risk: Rolling back the rules could make some insurers pull back again.
Rates may still rise either way.

items.headline: California asks insurers how they use AI; public workshop set for Dec. 15
items.caption: Regulators want to know how AI shapes insurance decisions and who oversees it. Insurer answers are due Dec. 30.
detail: The California Department of Insurance launched a Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence Survey. It asks how insurers use AI, how they govern it, the role of outside vendors, and how AI changes their operations.
A virtual public workshop is set for Dec. 15 at 10 a.m. Topics include transparency, fairness, privacy, human oversight, and insurer responsibility for vendors' technology.
Responses are due Dec. 30. The department will use what it learns to decide whether new consumer protections or rules are needed.
money: If an insurer denies a claim or raises your rate, you can ask what data and tools drove the decision.
Consumers can join the Dec. 15 workshop to share experiences with automated decisions.
Keep records of claims and calls; they help if you dispute an automated outcome.
risk: Survey results may take months to become rules.
New rules could add costs passed on to policyholders.

items.headline: 8-year-old Haitian boy held by ICE for about two weeks is returned to his family
items.caption: San Diego lawmakers had demanded his release in a letter to DHS and HHS. The report includes no comment from federal agencies.
detail: An 8-year-old Haitian third-grader taken into ICE custody about two weeks earlier was returned to his family around 1 p.m. Monday, KPBS reported. His uncle was among the relatives who received him.

San Diego's Democratic House members and California's two senators had written to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asking for his return. Rep. Juan Vargas met the family at the release.
The Haitian Bridge Alliance helped advocate for the child. The report did not include a statement from ICE, DHS or HHS on why he was detained.
money: Families with mixed immigration status can set up a written plan for who cares for children in an emergency.
Free or low-cost legal aid groups can review your case; check accredited nonprofits before paying anyone.
Keep key documents and copies in a safe, known place.
risk: Details of why the child was detained have not been released.

items.headline: Houthis launch drones at Mecca and Riyadh as they push toward Aden, Saudi coalition says
items.caption: The Saudi-led coalition reported two drones Monday. Houthi forces also gained ground on Yemen's south coast.

visual.title: Yemen war, Monday
items: Coalition: two Houthi drones launched at Mecca and Riyadh
Houthis reported about 60 km from Aden
Saudi media name a new coalition commander
Houthis already hold Yemen's whole Red Sea coast

detail: The Saudi-led coalition said Monday that Yemen's Houthis launched two drones at Mecca and Riyadh. Reports did not say whether they hit anything. Saudi state media also announced a new commander for the anti-Houthi coalition.
Houthi forces advanced along Yemen's southern coast and were reported about 60 km from Aden, the seat of the interim government.

The Iran-backed group controls Sanaa and all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and has declared a blockade of Saudi Arabia, hitting its ships and oil sites. The UN says the fighting has killed more than 1,600 people.
money: Attacks near Saudi oil sites can jolt oil prices even when supply looks ample; avoid chasing short spikes.
Shipping disruption in the Red Sea can raise costs for imported goods over time.
Energy funds can swing on Gulf headlines; keep any position sized for volatility.
risk: A strike on major oil facilities could lift prices quickly.
Battlefield claims are hard to verify.

items.headline: Nasdaq is now in a correction, more than 10% below its October 6 record
items.caption: Chip stocks led Monday's drop, with the semiconductor index down 5.3%. Losers beat gainers about 3.5 to 1 on the NYSE.

visual.title: Monday's damage, by the numbers
visual.foot: Nvidia reports Tuesday after the bell.

detail: The Nasdaq closed at 24,509.76 on Monday, down 2.49%. That leaves it more than 10% below its October 6 record close, which traders call a correction.
Chips were hit hardest. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 5.3%. Intel and Micron each dropped more than 7%, Nebius fell 7.6%, Dell lost 7% and Super Micro fell 6.9%.
The selling was broad. On the Nasdaq, 3,697 stocks fell and 1,131 rose, with 489 new 52-week lows against 51 new highs. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 5.12% from 5.15%.
money: If you buy funds on a schedule, a correction means each dollar buys more shares.
Check how much of your portfolio sits in chip and AI stocks; many index funds are now tech-heavy.
Rebalancing back to your target mix can lock in gains from bonds or cash that held up.
risk: Corrections can deepen into bear markets (down 20% or more).
Nvidia's results Tuesday could swing the whole sector either way.
